issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: At 72, Margaret had always been a diligent and meticulous network engineer, but it was an incident at a crowded bus station five years ago that changed her life forever. She witnessed a violent altercation between two strangers, which ended with one of them being rushed to the hospital. The trauma of that event lingered, and Margaret found herself increasingly uneasy in crowded places, including public transport. Even thinking about certain conversation topics related to violence or crime would send her mind racing back to that fateful day. As she began to avoid bus riding and crowded areas like shopping centers, Margaret convinced herself that these precautions were necessary because the world was a dangerous place. She became hypervigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats, and started to see herself as an outsider, no longer part of the carefree crowd. Her friends and family noticed her growing wariness but couldn't understand why she was so adamant about avoiding certain places and topics. Margaret's efforts to cope with these fears led her to adopt a strict regimen of positive thinking. She forced herself to focus only on good thoughts, hoping to counteract the dark ones that seemed to seep in whenever she encountered triggers like crowded buses or conversations about violence. However, this coping mechanism only served to heighten her sense of being an outsider; it felt like she was living in a bubble, separate from everyone else. Avoiding the site where the incident occurred became an all-consuming goal for Margaret. She would go out of her way to take detours, even if it meant adding extra time to her commute. Her loved ones found this behavior perplexing but tried to be supportive. Yet, despite these efforts, Margaret's anxiety only intensified. The more she avoided certain situations, the more convinced she became that they were indeed treacherous. The connections between her fears and behaviors became a self-reinforcing cycle. As she shunned crowded areas, she felt an increasing sense of unease whenever she was forced to confront them - on public transport or in conversation. Her attempts at positive thinking only made her more aware of the dangers lurking beneath the surface, which in turn fueled her hypervigilance. As Margaret's avoidance behaviors became more entrenched, they began to affect her occupation as a network engineer. She would decline projects that required her to travel to crowded areas or meet with clients who worked in fields related to crime or violence. Her colleagues started to notice her withdrawal and wondered if she was simply burned out or if something more serious was at play. It wasn't until Margaret's husband pointed out the toll her behaviors were taking on their relationship - they could no longer attend social events together, and their conversations had become strained - that she realized she needed help. What finally brought her to seek therapy was not just the accumulation of her symptoms but also the crushing weight of living in constant fear. As she sat in the therapist's office, Margaret expressed a deep longing to be free from this cycle of anxiety and avoidance, to find a way to confront the world without being crippled by her own perceptions. Margaret's story is one of how trauma can insidiously weave its way into everyday life, warping perceptions and behaviors until even the smallest triggers feel like major threats. Her narrative arc - from witnessing a traumatic event to developing a complex web of avoidance and fear - serves as a poignant reminder that seeking help requires more than just recognizing symptoms; it demands confronting the deep-seated fears that drive them.
